module: Start here: what the GDPR covers

lesson.title: Pseudonymised and anonymous data
lesson.summary: Tell pseudonymised data, which is still personal data, from anonymous data, which is outside the GDPR.

prerequisites.reason: Pseudonymised data stays personal data because extra information can still identify the person.

blocks: **Pseudonymisation** means processing personal data so that it can no longer be linked to a specific person without additional information. That additional information must be kept separately and protected (Article 4(5)).
A typical example is replacing names with codes and storing the list of codes somewhere else.

Pseudonymised data is **still personal data**. Recital 26 says that data which could be linked back to a person using additional information should be treated as information about an identifiable person.
So the GDPR still applies in full.
**Anonymous information** does not relate to an identified or identifiable person. Personal data can also be made anonymous so that the person is no longer identifiable (recital 26).
The GDPR does not concern anonymous information. That includes anonymous information used for statistics or research (recital 26).

Whether data is truly anonymous is a test, not a label. Recital 26 says to consider all the means reasonably likely to be used to identify someone, including the cost, the time and the technology available.
It also mentions "technological developments". Data that is anonymous today might become identifiable later, so the assessment needs to be reviewed.
Sunfield sends its order data to an analyst. It replaces customer names with codes, and the manager keeps the code list in a locked file. That data is **pseudonymised**, so the GDPR still applies.
Sunfield also publishes "pre-orders per shop per month". If no customer can be singled out from those totals, they are anonymous.

blocks.text: **Sunfield Bakery is invented** for this course. Any resemblance to a real business is accidental.

blocks: If pseudonymised data is still covered, why bother? Because the GDPR itself names pseudonymisation as a protective measure, in Article 25(1) and Article 32(1)(a). Later lessons explain both articles.

questions.prompt: Sunfield replaces customer names with codes and keeps the code list separately. Is the result personal data?

options.blocks: Yes, it is pseudonymised and can be linked back
options.reason: Recital 26 treats it as information about an identifiable person.

options.blocks: No, the codes make it anonymous
options.reason: The key still allows the data to be linked back, so it is not anonymous.

options.blocks: Only if the code list is ever lost
options.reason: The data is personal data regardless of what happens to the key.

variants.prompt: After names are swapped for codes, with the key kept elsewhere, does the GDPR still apply?

options.blocks: No, the codes make it anonymous
options.reason: The key still allows the data to be linked back, so it is not anonymous.

options.blocks: Only if the code list is ever lost
options.reason: The data is personal data regardless of what happens to the key.

options.blocks: Yes, it is pseudonymised and can be linked back
options.reason: Recital 26 treats it as information about an identifiable person.

options.blocks: The names have been deleted from the file
options.reason: Other details may still single someone out.

options.blocks: The file is encrypted with a password
options.reason: Whoever holds the password can still read the data.

options.blocks: No one can identify the person by any means reasonably likely to be used
options.reason: That is the recital 26 test for anonymity.

variants.prompt: When is information outside the GDPR because it is anonymous?

options.blocks: The file is encrypted with a password
options.reason: Whoever holds the password can still read the data.

options.blocks: No one can identify the person by any means reasonably likely to be used
options.reason: That is the recital 26 test for anonymity.

options.blocks: The names have been deleted from the file
options.reason: Other details may still single someone out.

questions.prompt: Why should a business review an earlier decision that some data is anonymous?

options.blocks: The GDPR requires consent before anonymising
options.reason: Recital 26 sets an identifiability test. It says nothing about consent.

options.blocks: Technology develops, and identification may become reasonably likely
options.reason: Recital 26 says to consider technological developments.

options.blocks: Anonymous data automatically expires after one year
options.reason: The GDPR sets no such expiry. It is invented.
